newsitem.title: zaire: RWANDA SAYS ONLY 55,000 HUTU REFUGEES IN ZAIRE.
newsitem.headline: RWANDA SAYS ONLY 55,000 HUTU REFUGEES IN ZAIRE.

text.p: The head of Rwanda's repatriation commission said on Friday only 55,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees remained in Zaire and a U.N. airlift would take nearly half of them home within 10 days.
Ephraim Kabaija, whose duty is to oversee reintegration of over two million Hutu refugees into Rwanda, said estimates of the number of refugees still in Zaire were wildly exaggerated.
"There has never been a census, they have never been counted," Kabaija said as he left the northeastern Zairean capital of Kisangani after talks with U.N. refugee agency UNHCR officials.

"The figures you are talking about are feeding figures and everybody knows the refugees exaggerate these figures to get UNHCR estimates some 300,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees are unaccounted for in Zaire since they fled their camps in the east shortly after the start of a revolt by Tutsi-dominated rebels last October.
Rwanda has expressed support for the revolt by the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL). Zaire's government has accused Rwandan troops to fight alongside the rebels.
Kabaija said 25,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees -- the remaining population of the Kasese and Biaro camps south of Kisangani -- would be airlifted home within 10 days.
"Weather permitting and taking into account logistics, the UNHCR told me they can do the job in 10 days," he said.

UNHCR officials confirmed they believed they could airlift the 25,000 near Kisangani within 10 days but disputed the estimates of those remaining and that its figures for Biaro and Kasese were exaggerated. They declined further comment.
Aid officials said some 85,000 were camped at Biaro and Kasese until attacks by local villagers and AFDL rebels almost three weeks ago forced them to flee into the surrounding forest.
Some 40,000 returned to the camps in the last two weeks and UNHCR has repatriated nearly 15,000 since an airlift from Kisangani started on April 27. Some 1,750 flew home on Friday.
Kabaija said 1,000 refugees might have died in the camp attacks and a train stampede on Sunday which killed 92 refugees.
"All together, only a thousand of them have been knocked off...The rest have all come back. These are the real figures."
UNHCR on Monday blamed a breakdown in coordination with rebel authorities for the death of the refugees who were crushed or suffocated to death on a train on its way to Kisangani.

Kabaija said refugees interviewed on their return to Rwanda has said the camp attacks were carried out by villagers and militiamen. Asked to explain what he meant by militias, Kabaija said: "You know, Zaireans, but in civilian clothes."
He said at his meeting with UNHCR officials, the rebels were cleared of any blame for the train disaster and UNHCR, the U.N. World Food Programme and railway authorities were responsible.
Asked whether he had pressed AFDL officials to allow aid agencies more access to areas where refugees may be hiding, Kabaija said such a request was not needed.
"It always comes back to the figures," he said. "Believe me there are not that many left."
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila had promised aid agencies free access to all areas under his control but U.N. officials still cannot go much more than 40 km (25 miles) south of Kisangani.
The refugees fled to Zaire in 1994 to escape reprisals for the genocide of over 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus. More than 100,000 Hutus are held in Rwanda awaiting trial for the mass slaughter.
